text: Merata Mita CNZM (19 June 1942 – 31 May 2010) was a New Zealand filmmaker, producer, and writer who played a pivotal role in the development of the Māori screen industry. She was the first indigenous woman and the first woman in New Zealand to solely write and direct a dramatic feature film, Mauri (1988). Born on 19 June 1942 in Maketu, Bay of Plenty, she was the third of nine children and grew up in a traditional rural Māori environment belonging to the iwi Ngāti Pikiao and Ngāi Te Rangi. She taught at Kawerau College for eight years, where she used film and video to engage high school students, many of whom were Māori and Pacific Islander, through oral storytelling and artistic expression, sparking her interest in filmmaking. Initially working as a liaison for film crews and later as a sound assistant and sound recordist, she gained recognition within the film industry and began a long career in film and television. In 1990, she moved to Hawaii and taught documentary filmmaking at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. Her debut feature film, Mauri (1988), challenged mainstream narratives by asserting Māori cultural sovereignty and honoring the Treaty of Waitangi, with its title meaning cycles of life and spiritual connection to the land. The film's hill is described as having filmic agency, representing the "mauri" or life force, and is central to the concept of "Fourth Cinema"—a term coined by Barry Barclay for indigenous cinema created by indigenous filmmakers for indigenous audiences. Prior to the 1970s, Māori were largely portrayed by male Pakeha filmmakers in ways that reduced their culture to colonial myths. A 37% increase in Māori urban residency from 1945 to 1966 contributed to cultural disconnection and loss of traditions, leading to the Māori Renaissance, a movement to preserve identity. Mita’s films were politically engaged, reflecting her belief that all aspects of life are political, and she actively participated in struggles such as Maori land occupations, anti-apartheid, and anti-racist movements. She co-directed To Love A Māori (1972) with Ramai Te Miha Hayward and directed landmark documentaries including Bastion Point: Day 507 (1980), which was the only media access permitted by Ngāti Whātua during their land protest, and Patu! (1983), about the 1981 South African Springboks rugby tours, as well as Hotere (2001) on artist Ralph Hotere and the music video Waka for Che Fu. In 1998, a documentary on her life, Rangatira: Merata Mita – Making Waves, was directed by Hinewehi Mohi. In 2014, NZ on Air funded a biographical film, Te Taki A Merata Mita – How Mum Decolonised The Screen, to be directed by her son Heperi Mita, which was accepted into the Sundance Film Festival in 2019. Mita mentored indigenous filmmakers internationally through organizations such as the Sundance Film Festival's Native Film Initiative, the National Geographic All Roads Indigenous Film Festival, and the Pacific Islanders in Communications consortium, and in 2016, the Sundance Institute established the Merata Mita Fellowship for indigenous filmmakers globally. She received numerous awards, including the Amiens International Film Festival's MRAP Award for Patu! (1983), the Rimini Film Festival's Best Film for Mauri (1989), the Flaherty Seminar's Leo Dratfield Award (1996), the Taos Film Festival's Mountain Award (1999), the Te Waka Toi "Making a difference" Award (2009), and was appointed a Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the 2010 New Year Honours. She was also nominated for the Asia Pacific Screen Awards' Best Children's Feature Film (2010) and the Aotearoa Film and Television Awards' Best Director – Television Documentary (2011). The National Geographic All Roads Festival established the Merata Mita Award in 2010 to honor a legacy of outstanding storytelling. Mita had seven children: Rafer, Richard, Rhys, Lars, Awatea, Eruera, and Hepi; her fourth son, Lars, died at 11 months. Her son Hepi Mita produced the documentary Merata: How Mum Decolonised the Screen, released in 2018. Mita died suddenly on 31 May 2010 after collapsing outside the studios of Māori Television. She directed or collaborated on numerous films and television shows.
